story: In 1987, a young lieutenant colonel named Sitiveni Rabuka walked into Fiji's parliament with masked soldiers and overthrew the elected government, the first of two coups he led that year in the name of indigenous Fijian dominance. Thirty-five years later he became prime minister again, this time by winning an election, and has spent his second career trying to cast himself as a reconciler, including backing a truth and reconciliation commission into the coups he himself began. In 2026, as Fiji prepared for an election due by early 2027, the old question came back: can the country move past its military men?

The year was rough for his government. Two deputy prime ministers resigned after being charged by the anti-corruption commission FICAC, one of them Biman Prasad, leader of a coalition partner, prompting claims Rabuka was using the agency against rivals, which he denied (Mai TV). A High Court ruling in favour of the anti-corruption chief he had dismissed embarrassed him further. Opposition figure Savenaca Narube, a former central bank governor, told voters not to "choose military people" to lead again; Rabuka, now 77, replied that Narube did not understand democracy (Fiji Sun). The stakes reach beyond Fiji: Rabuka has pulled the country closer to Australia and away from the Chinese ties his predecessor built.
briefing.power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 55-seat parliament, elected by open-list proportional representation in a single national constituency; the president, chosen by parliament, is largely ceremonial. The military has historically acted as a political arbiter.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka (People's Alliance), leading a three-party coalition since 2022.
